item.content:encoded:
Hidden ways people-pleasing can affect your relationships and self-esteem
Content creator Murugi Munyi has sparked a conversation about people-pleasing after reflecting on how the habit affected her over the years.
In a personal reflection shared on Thursday, November 12, 2026, Murugi spoke about her journey towards personal growth, highlighting the importance of recognising behaviours that may prevent individuals from prioritising themselves.
Her experience brings attention to a habit that many people mistake for kindness but which can quietly affect relationships, confidence and emotional well-being.
People-pleasing often involves struggling to say no, avoiding disagreements and constantly seeking approval to feel accepted. While helping others is healthy, repeatedly putting their needs before your own can create an unhealthy pattern.
When kindness turns into emotional exhaustion
One hidden effect of people-pleasing is becoming emotionally drained from constantly trying to keep everyone happy.
You may find yourself accepting responsibilities you cannot manage, offering help when exhausted or apologising even when you have done nothing wrong.
Over time, this can create resentment, especially when the effort you put into maintaining relationships is not reciprocated.
In some cases, people may also struggle to communicate their feelings because they fear upsetting those around them.
How it affects relationships and self-worth
People-pleasing can create relationships where one person continually compromises while the other becomes accustomed to having their way.
When someone repeatedly suppresses their opinions to avoid conflict, their needs may go unnoticed. This can make it difficult to recognise relationships where respect and consideration are lacking.
Constantly seeking approval can also weaken self-confidence. Individuals may begin measuring their worth through compliments, acceptance and how others respond to their decisions.
They may also struggle to make independent choices, fearing that expressing their preferences could disappoint people around them.
Learning to put yourself first
Breaking the habit does not mean becoming inconsiderate. It starts with identifying personal needs, communicating honestly and learning to say no without excessive guilt.
Building healthy boundaries also allows people to maintain relationships without sacrificing their identity.
People can begin by recognising situations where they agree out of fear of rejection rather than genuine willingness. Taking time before committing to requests can also help them make decisions that reflect their priorities.
Ultimately, genuine connections should make room for mutual respect, honesty and individual needs. Learning to prioritise yourself does not mean caring less about others; it means recognising that your well-being matters too.
